To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
we used SWITCH to immunolablel whole brains and created a spatiatemporal map of beta-amyoid (Aβ) in the 5xTAD mouse.

we have developed a method to immunolabel large tissue volumes and that this method reveals subcortical structures are the first to be susceptible to amyloid accumulation in mice, and that this subcortical accumulation correlates with neuronal dysfunction.

1) subcortical structures are the primary site of Aβ accumulation in AD, 2) early Aβ accumulation in these structures is correlated with neuronal hyper-exitability, and 3) Aβ accumulation can be reduced by a pharmacogenetic manipulation.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding how brain networks change in response to amyloid accumulation and how these changes relate to cognitive deficits.
understanding how brain regions become susceptible to Aβ deposition and how these regions contribute to the development of AD pathology.
understanding how the brain works and how it goes wrong in disease.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
SWITCH immunolabeling of whole brain can be used to show that subcortically located brain regions are susceptible to A β accumulation in mice.
this work provides new insights into early amyloid accumulation and neuronal dysfunction in the brain of mice and may be applicable to human Alzheimer’s disease.
the mammillary body and subcortices of mice are susceptible to A β accumulation and that A β accumulation in the mammillothalamic tract is linked to neuronal excitability.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
subcortically-mediated brain alterations may contribute to early brain dysfunction in Alzheimer's disease.
we used SWITCH to map amyloid deposition in 5XFAD mice and identified subcortical structures that are susceptible to early amyloid pathology.
subcortically-mediated susceptibility is a key factor in early AD pathogenesis.
The main takeaway from our work is that
subcortically located memory structures are the most vulnerable to early Aβ deposition and that Aβ accumulation may be linked to neuronal hyper-excitable activity.
large volume immunohistochemistry is an effective way to identify regions that are susceptible to amyloid pathology.
the mammillary body may be an early and important region for amyloid pathology in Alzheimer's Disease and that subcortically located memory structures may show early vulnerability to Aβ accumulation.
